name: Black salve

lead: Black salve is a topical escharotic: a paste that chemically destroys the skin it touches and leaves a dead scab (an eschar). People in alternative-health circles use it at home on moles, skin tags, cysts and other lesions, with the appearance goal of making a visible growth fall off without surgery.

Proponents describe it as a natural treatment that targets only abnormal tissue. Published reviews, which are mostly case reports and laboratory work, describe the paste as damaging to healthy and abnormal tissue alike, with scarring as a common outcome and no controlled clinical trials of cosmetic or curative results.

paras: Products are sold as tins or jars of dark paste online, often under names like drawing salve. Users describe dabbing it onto a single lesion, covering it, and waiting weeks for a scab to form and lift away, leaving an open wound that heals gradually.

Case reports describe pain, ulceration, infection, permanent scars, loss of tissue (including parts of the nose) and cancers that persisted or spread after treatment. Regulators in the US and Australia have issued warnings, and sale is illegal in Australia. Dermatology bodies advise having any new or changing lesion examined before it is treated.

angle.text: Users apply it to moles, tags and other blemishes hoping to remove them at home. Published case reports describe the resulting wound as often leaving a scar or deformity larger than the original lesion.

lead: Black salve is a dark topical paste, typically built around bloodroot (Sanguinaria canadensis) and often zinc chloride, that is applied to the skin to chemically destroy a lesion. It belongs to the escharotics, pastes that burn tissue and leave a scab-like eschar [1][2]. Brands and names include Cansema, drawing salve, black ointment and bloodroot salve [3].

In appearance terms, people use it at home on moles, skin tags, warts, cysts and other visible growths, hoping the lesion will slough off and leave clear skin without an excision or clinic visit. Vendors promote it as natural and selective for abnormal cells, and testimonials circulate on alternative-health sites, video platforms and social media [4][2][5]. A 2015 analysis of popular YouTube videos on skin cancer found black salve promoted as a home remedy in 27.7 percent of consumer-made videos and in none of the professional ones, with those videos drawing over three million views [6].

Related escharotic pastes have a medical history: 19th-century surgeons used bloodroot and zinc pastes, and Frederic Mohs used a zinc chloride paste in the 1930s in the work that became Mohs micrographic surgery [3][7]. Published literature on modern black salve is reviews, case reports and laboratory work, which describe indiscriminate tissue destruction, frequent scarring or disfigurement, and cases where an underlying cancer persisted [8][1][4][9]. The US FDA, Australia's TGA and dermatology bodies have warned against it [3][5].
infobox: Sale illegal in Australia; FDA warnings in the US

paras: Black salve has no standard formula. Many products combine bloodroot extract with zinc chloride and fillers, and reviews note that the corrosive activity comes from sanguinarine and zinc chloride rather than the inert base [1]. Sanguinarine is the main alkaloid of bloodroot and is toxic to animal cells, which is the basis of the eschar it produces [10].
Products appear under many labels, including drawing salve and bloodroot ointment, and are sold through independent websites and online marketplaces [2].

Bloodroot is a perennial flowering plant of eastern North America whose rhizome is rich in sanguinarine, an alkaloid that colours the sap red [10]. Wikipedia describes sanguinarine as killing animal cells by blocking the Na+/K+-ATPase membrane pump, which is the basis of the eschar it forms on skin [10]. Black salve recipes usually add zinc chloride, and sometimes chaparral or other herbs; none of these is selective, and manufacturing is largely unregulated, so strength and purity are unknown [3].

Laboratory work indicates that sanguinarine destroys healthy skin cells at concentrations above about 5 micromolar [8]. Reviews have also examined theoretical risks, including epidemic dropsy and the carcinogenic potential of sanguinarine, neither of which has been established from black salve use [11][12].

Bloodroot was used by Native American peoples as an emetic, respiratory aid and dye, and escharotic pastes were part of mainstream skin treatment in the 19th century, including a bloodroot and zinc paste sold by the surgeon Jesse Fell from 1850 [3][10]. In 1938 the surgeon Frederic Mohs developed microscopically controlled surgery for skin cancer, originally using a zinc chloride and bloodroot paste left on the wound overnight, then removing the fixed tissue and examining it under the microscope the next day [7]. Wikipedia notes that the later fresh-tissue technique with frozen sections allowed same-day surgery with less tissue destruction and similar cure rates, and distinguishes Mohs's brief, microscope-checked use from the long, unsupervised use of black salve and Hoxsey's paste [7].

A 1955 Time article described a woman whose nose was destroyed after a healer applied a salve to a condition that was not cancer, and Duke surgeons rebuilt it [3]. Dentistry also used bloodroot extracts: the toothpaste and mouthwash Viadent, which contained them, was withdrawn from the North American market over cancer concerns [10].

The brand most associated with modern black salve is Cansema, sold by Alpha Omega Labs, founded in 1995 by Greg Caton (1956-2021) [13]. Caton earlier founded the multi-level marketing company Nutrition for Life; Alpha Omega sold over 300 alternative-health products, and the FDA moved against it in 2003 [13]. In 2004 Caton pleaded guilty to weapons possession by a felon, defrauding customers and violating FDA regulations, and was sentenced to 33 months [13]. He was released in 2006 on probation, moved to Ecuador in 2007, was found in violation of probation, was listed by Interpol in 2008 and arrested in Ecuador in December 2009; he kept selling products online and appeared in a 2017 segment on the Dr. Oz show on black salve, and died on 15 December 2021 [13]. His supporters' outlets described the arrest as FDA persecution, while the agency listed Cansema among fake cancer cures [3][13].

Other brands named by Wikipedia include Black Ointment from Dr. Christopher's Original Formulas and Herb Veil 8 from Altered States [3]. Sellers rely heavily on testimonials; the product is often labelled for uses such as drawing out splinters, and the zinc chloride is synthetic, whatever the 'natural' framing [2][3].

Vendors and users say the salve pulls out or kills only abnormal cells, is natural, and leaves little scarring. A review of vendor claims examined natural credentials, tumour specificity and cosmetic outcome, and concluded from laboratory and histology data that the paste probably harms normal tissue, while some cancer cell lines appear relatively resistant [4]. One reviewer quoted by CBS New York in 2018 wrote 'The skin will die and the tumor will fall out' [5].

Community framing often pairs black salve with distrust of conventional dermatology and with the view that a corrosive paste is a do-it-yourself equivalent of surgery [4][2]. By 2018 some people were using it on pets [3].

Products are sold as tins or jars of dark paste online, often under names like drawing salve [2]. Users describe dabbing it onto a single lesion, covering it, and waiting weeks for a scab to form and lift away, leaving an open wound that heals gradually [2]. Dermatologists note the depth of the burn cannot be controlled, which is the reason reviews describe it as hazardous without supervision [1][5].

No controlled clinical trials have tested black salve. The clinical literature is case reports and series, which report suboptimal therapeutic and cosmetic outcomes [8][1]. A series of 16 cases examined pathology after application [14]. One case study described a thin melanoma treated with the salve that persisted and later metastasised [15], and other reports describe deformity after self-treatment [16][9]. In a 14-patient case series for basal-cell carcinoma reported by Wikipedia, five needed conventional treatment afterwards and one died [3]; Wikipedia contrasts this with a Mohs surgery cure rate of about 99.5 percent for basal-cell carcinoma [3]. Mohs's own paste is described as differing from black salve because it was used briefly and followed by microscopic examination [7].

Documented problems include pain, ulcers that heal over months, infection, scarring, loss of tissue, and treatment failure with later spread of a cancer [1][15][16]. A case report describes use on a neck cyst with significant tissue damage [17], and a 2023 Cureus case report describes black salve as a dangerous corrosive presented as alternative medicine [18]. Rare complications described by Wikipedia include burn-through of the skin into the large bowel [3].

In Australia in 2018, Helen Lawson died after applying black salve to her abdomen for ovarian cancer on the advice of a self-described healer, Dennis Wayne Jensen; her wounds became too large for surgery, and in 2019 Victoria's Health Complaints Commissioner permanently barred Jensen from providing products claimed to treat cancer [3]. Dr. Kavita Mariwalla told CBS New York in 2018 that the burn cannot really be controlled, and advised against doing skin cancer treatment at home [5]. The American Academy of Dermatology urges people to see a dermatologist before using home remedies for skin cancer [3].

Sale of black salve is illegal in Australia and the TGA has issued consumer warnings; it also found organisations including the Australian Vaccination-Skeptics Network and individuals in breach of advertising rules for promoting it [19][3]. In the United States the FDA listed Cansema among 187 fake cancer cures, and has issued warning letters and taken enforcement action; several other countries have also recommended against its use [3]. Sellers often label products for non-cancer uses [2].

lore.intro: In alternative-health and some DIY-skin communities, black salve is discussed as a way to remove moles, tags and lesions at home, often alongside distrust of conventional dermatology [4][2][6].
